events.event: Islamic biographical tradition places Muhammad's first revelatory experience around this year. Historical reporting can document that this is the tradition, not establish an angelic visitation or revelation as an objective event.
events.place: Mount Hira area, outside Mecca (location in the traditional account)
events.locator: Jonathan E. Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Introduction, excerpt p. 4 / PDF lines 128–149: the account places meditation outside Mecca in 610 and frames the revelation and Gabriel as the Muslim narrative; it dates the Meccan period 610–622.
events.qualification: The date and setting are reported through later religious biography. Phrase as 'tradition dates/recounts'; do not narrate revelation, divine speech, or supernatural claims as independently verified fact.

events.date: 610s; public preaching often conventionally dated c. 613
events.event: A small circle of followers formed around Muhammad's preaching in Mecca; the exact chronology and first adherents are disputed in the transmitted accounts.
events.locator: Gerald R. Hawting, The Formation of Islam, chapter “The Origins of the Muslim Community,” lines 279–282: explicitly situates the early prophetic career in the Muslim narrative and the origins of the community in Arabia. Compare Brockopp, Introduction, pp. 4–5, which notes uncertainty over who first joined Muhammad's intimate circle (PDF lines 471–480).
events.qualification: The Cambridge chapter is an overview and explicitly attributes its account to Muslim origin narratives; it supports a cautious broad milestone, not a precise year, headcount, or fully settled institutional community.

events.event: Some early followers are reported to have emigrated from Mecca to the Christian kingdom of Aksum/Abyssinia amid worsening hostility.
events.place: From Mecca to the Kingdom of Aksum (Abyssinia; destination location not specified more precisely by the consulted passage)
events.locator: Jonathan E. Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Introduction, pp. 7–8 / PDF lines 496–502: describes emigration to Christian Abyssinia as part of the traditional evidence for increasing conflict and notes that the tradition preserves accounts of hardship.
events.qualification: The consulted scholarly passage confirms the episode but does not establish 615 as an exact date. The motive, group size, routes, and sequence are known through later Muslim reports; avoid precise numbers and dramatized speeches.

events.date: Traditionally c. 616–619; start and end dates uncertain
events.event: Later Muslim accounts describe a social and commercial boycott against Muhammad's clan, which continued protecting him; Cambridge's scholarly synthesis identifies a boycott against his clan but does not certify all later details of its duration or terms.
events.place: Mecca; the traditional account associates the confinement with the Shiʿb Abi Talib area
events.locator: Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Introduction, pp. 7–8 / PDF lines 496–502: identifies a boycott against Muhammad's clan and explicitly frames suffering accounts as tradition.
events.qualification: Use 'later accounts report' and avoid asserting the exact 616–619 span, specific written pact details, or the valley's precise archaeological location as settled facts; those details are not established by the consulted passage.

events.event: Accounts of the first Aqaba meeting describe a small group from Yathrib meeting Muhammad during pilgrimage and accepting his religious invitation; this is presented in scholarship through the traditional narrative.
events.place: Al-Aqaba, on the outskirts of Mecca near the pilgrimage route/Mina
events.locator: Faisal Shuayb, “Who's Better than God to Rule? An Inquiry into the Formation of the First Islamic State (622–32 CE),” doctoral dissertation, discussion of the Aqaba pledges, PDF excerpt reproduced in search result: describes a first meeting with six Khazraj men during Hajj, followed by their return to Yathrib.
events.qualification: The dissertation recounts classical Islamic reports and itself notes differing enumerations of the pledges. The conventional c. 620 date and party details should remain attributed to those reports, not stated with documentary certainty.

events.event: A second reported Aqaba pledge involved a larger group from Yathrib; traditional accounts say Muhammad sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr to teach the new adherents there.
events.place: Al-Aqaba, Mecca; Mus'ab's reported mission was to Yathrib
events.locator: Shuayb, dissertation, Aqaba pledges discussion: the next year's group is described as twelve men, including Aws and Khazraj members, with Mus'ab ibn Umayr sent to Yathrib; source labels the first two pledge traditions and their sequence.
events.qualification: The exact year, headcount, and pledge wording derive from later sira reports and are not independently corroborated in this consulted passage. Avoid presenting invented dialogue or treating the numbers as certain.

events.date: 622 (traditional chronology; conventionally the second Aqaba pledge)
events.event: A further reported agreement at Aqaba connected the Yathrib group with a commitment to receive and protect Muhammad and his followers; its precise form and numbering vary across accounts and scholarship.
events.place: Al-Aqaba, Mecca, near the pilgrimage area
events.locator: Shuayb, dissertation, Aqaba pledges discussion: describes the next Hajj-season gathering as a group of roughly seventy Medinans and notes that scholars differ on whether pledge traditions should be counted as two or three.
events.qualification: Use the conventional label only with an attribution such as 'the pledge known in the traditional chronology as the second Aqaba pledge.' Its details are transmitted reports, not an independently preserved treaty text.

events.date: 622 CE (Hijra; exact day not needed here)
events.event: Muhammad and followers emigrated from Mecca to Yathrib, establishing a new community there; the migration became the epoch for the Muslim calendar.
events.place: Mecca to Yathrib (later Medina), western Arabia
events.locator: Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Introduction, pp. 7–8 / PDF lines 518–564: identifies the Hijra in 622 as a turning point, names Yathrib, and notes that the traditional exact arrival date is 12 Rabiʿ I / September 24, 622 while discussing the community's social setting.
events.qualification: The year and migration are broadly accepted historical markers; the exact traditional day and narrative particulars vary. Muhammad is a historical actor in the account, never a playable unit or a source of fabricated dialogue.

sources.title: Jonathan E. Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Cambridge University Press, excerpt
sources.consultedScope: Read Introduction excerpt pp. 4–5 / PDF lines 128–149 and 471–480: traditional account of first revelation and 610–622 periodization; notes disagreement in transmitted reports about Muhammad's earliest followers.

sources.title: Jonathan E. Brockopp (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Muhammad, Cambridge University Press, preview excerpt
sources.consultedScope: Read Introduction pp. 7–9 / PDF lines 496–564: scholarly synthesis of tradition about Abyssinian emigration and clan boycott, deaths of Abu Talib and Khadija in 619, Hijra in 622, traditional arrival-date claim, and caveats about source quality and competing narratives.

sources.title: Gerald R. Hawting, The Formation of Islam: The Making of a World Religion, Cambridge University Press, chapter “The Origins of the Muslim Community”
sources.consultedScope: Read the chapter overview, lines 279–282: dates the community's migration to Yathrib to 622 and explicitly qualifies the early Meccan career as depicted by Muslim-origin sources. Overview only; not used to support fine-grained chronology.

sources.title: Faisal Shuayb, “Who's Better than God to Rule? An Inquiry into the Formation of the First Islamic State (622–32 CE),” doctoral dissertation, University of California eScholarship
sources.consultedScope: Consulted dissertation search excerpt on the Aqaba pledges: outlines reported meetings, traditional party sizes, sending Mus'ab to Yathrib, and the scholarly disagreement on counting pledges. The details are treated as transmitted reports, not independent contemporary documentation.
